title: Waiting an hour (Mishnah Berakhot 5:1)
hookLine: the early pious waited an hour to focus before praying

lines: YOUR HEAD IS STILL IN THE LAST THING.
cards: You've done this. You sit down to do the important thing, the letter, the hard conversation, the prayer, and your head is still in the last thing. The email you didn't answer.
The song from the car. You start, and three sentences in you realize you haven't heard a word you said. The Mishnah, about eighteen hundred years ago, knew this problem well.
And it describes a group of people with a startling solution: before they prayed, they waited. Not a moment. An hour.

teach.b: The fifth chapter of tractate Berakhot opens like this, in paraphrase. One doesn't stand up to pray except with koved rosh, a heaviness of head: seriousness, weight, a mind that has settled. Then the example.
The chasidim ha-rishonim, the early pious ones, would wait one hour and then pray, so they could direct their hearts to their Father in heaven. And then the Mishnah turns up the intensity.
Once you've begun, even if a king greets you, don't answer. Even if a snake is wrapped around your heel, don't stop.
The rabbis later soften that last line for real danger, a scorpion, for instance, so don't take it as a dare. The point is the depth of the focus.
The Talmud, discussing this Mishnah, finds a hint for the hour in a verse from Psalm 84: "Happy are they that dwell in Thy house." Dwelling first, before the praise.

teach.h: THE EARLY PIOUS WAITED AN HOUR.
teach.b: And it adds that these pious ones waited an hour before, prayed for an hour, and lingered an hour after.
Nine hours a day, if you pray three times. Someone in the Talmud asks the obvious question: so when did they get any work done?
The answer given is that because they were so devoted, their study and their work were blessed. Nobody expects that schedule of a person with a job and a family.
What survived into everyday law is the principle, not the hour.
The codes ask for kavanah, intention, above all in the Amidah's first blessing, and a short silent pause before beginning is a common habit. The early pious set the bar at an hour.
Most people keep the direction: arrive first, then speak.

how: Jewish law asks for kavanah, focused intention, especially in the Amidah; the psalms and blessings of the morning service serve as a warm-up, and some people pause in silence for a moment before beginning to pray.

o: a heavy headache that excuses you from praying
a settled, serious mind before you begin to pray
the head covering worn by men while praying

games.q: inside waiting an hour — tap the pairs.

s: the Mishnah requires everyone to wait an hour before praying
it describes what the early pious did; the lasting rule is to pray with a settled mind.
the Talmud says they waited an hour before, prayed an hour, and lingered an hour after
and it asks how they ever got their work done.
the rabbis let you stop praying for real danger
they soften the snake line for genuine danger like a scorpion.

games.q: you're one of the early pious ones. it's time to pray. what do you do first?
o: start right away, before the mind wanders.
wait an hour, to direct your heart.
games.why: they waited an hour, so they could direct their hearts to their Father in heaven.

practice: For the first minute, start nothing: let the last thing drain out of your head, like sediment settling in a glass of water.
Then begin something that matters, a prayer if you pray, or a single clear thought about what you want today to hold, and start only when you're actually here.

wordCard.voice: Koved rosh. A heaviness of head: the settled seriousness the Mishnah asks for before prayer, which led the early pious to wait an hour first.

orig.note: Hebrew: heaviness of head, the settled seriousness the Mishnah asks for before prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: focus first. The hour was theirs; the direction can be yours. Day six hundred thirty-four, done.
